title: Title, date and publication
short: Written in 1916 after the Easter Rising (24–29 April), privately printed in 25 copies, published only in October 1920.
body: The Easter Rising began on Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, when Irish Volunteers and the Irish Citizen Army seized buildings in Dublin and proclaimed an Irish Republic; it was suppressed within a week, and fifteen leaders were executed in May (a sixteenth, Roger Casement, was hanged in August). Yeats began the poem soon after; he wrote to Lady Gregory on 11 May that he was trying to write a poem on the executed men, and the finished poem is dated 25 September 1916. Clement Shorter privately printed twenty-five copies for distribution among friends. It was first published in the New Statesman (23 October 1920) and collected in Michael Robartes and the Dancer (1921).

title: Structure and numbers
short: Four stanzas of 16, 24, 16 and 24 lines, widely read as encoding the date of the Rising (24 April 1916, the fourth month).
body: The poem's stanzas have sixteen, twenty-four, sixteen and twenty-four lines respectively. Commentators have pointed out that the numbers match the year 1916 and the date (24 April), with four stanzas for the fourth month. The lines are mostly three-stress, a short, conversational measure that gives the poem a restrained, sober tone. Stanzas 1, 2 and 4 end with the refrain; the third stanza, with its image of the stone, stands outside the refrain.

anchor: From counter or desk among grey
title: counter or desk
short: The rebels came from ordinary jobs, shops and offices, a deliberately unheroic picture of them before the Rising.
body: The revolutionaries, seen before the Rising, were clerks, shop-assistants, teachers and minor officials, emerging 'at close of day' from 'counter or desk'. Yeats emphasises their ordinariness and his own condescension to them. The 'grey / Eighteenth-century houses' are the Georgian terraces of Dublin, the city of the Protestant Ascendancy, which Yeats later celebrated; 'grey' also suggests the dullness of ordinary life against their 'vivid faces'. The enjambment 'among grey / Eighteenth-century houses' spills the scene across the line.

title: Polite meaningless words
short: The phrase is repeated (ll. 6 and 8), enacting the empty social ritual it describes.
body: The repetition of 'Polite meaningless words' mimics the repetitive, automatic courtesy of casual encounters. The speaker admits his own disdain: he thought of 'a mocking tale or a gibe' to amuse a companion 'around the fire at the club', probably the Arts Club in Dublin which Yeats frequented. The confession places the speaker among those changed by the Rising: his own past attitude is exposed as shallow.

title: motley
short: Motley is the multicoloured costume of the professional fool: Dublin life before 1916 seemed a farce.
body: 'Motley' is the parti-coloured dress of the jester in Elizabethan drama, as in Jaques's 'Motley's the only wear' (As You Like It 2.7). Yeats implies that before the Rising both he and the rebels lived in a comic world where nothing was serious. The final stanza's 'Wherever green is worn' answers this line: the fool's motley has become the green of Irish nationalism. The 'casual comedy' of stanza 2 continues the theatrical metaphor.

title: A terrible beauty is born
short: The refrain's oxymoron fuses horror and splendour; Yeats used the phrase in a letter of May 1916.
body: The refrain recurs at the close of three stanzas. Its oxymoron joins 'terrible', inspiring terror, with 'beauty', in a way often compared to Burke's sublime, and the verb 'is born' implies a new life emerging from violence. In his letter of 11 May 1916 to Lady Gregory, Yeats wrote that 'terrible beauty has been born again', after Maud Gonne's remark that tragic dignity had returned to Ireland. Critics differ on whether the refrain celebrates the rebels' transfiguration or registers anxious ambivalence about violence; the poem's questions in stanza 4 suggest both. 'All changed, changed utterly' insists on the totality of the transformation.

title: That woman (Constance Markievicz)
short: Countess Constance Markievicz (née Gore-Booth, 1868–1927), a friend of Yeats's youth, sentenced to death but reprieved.
body: Constance Gore-Booth, of Lissadell, County Sligo, married the Polish Count Casimir Markievicz. She became a socialist and nationalist and was a second-in-command at St Stephen's Green in the Rising; her death sentence was commuted because she was a woman. Yeats contrasts her youthful beauty, when 'she rode to harriers' (hunted hares on horseback with a pack of harriers), with her later 'ignorant good will' and 'shrill' political voice. The judgement, coloured by Yeats's view that politics harmed women's beauty, recurs in 'In Memory of Eva Gore-Booth and Con Markiewicz' (written 1927, collected 1929).

title: rode to harriers
short: To hunt hares on horseback with a pack of harriers, the hunting dogs bred for the purpose.
body: A harrier is a hound used to hunt hares. To 'ride to harriers' (or 'to hounds') is to follow a hunt on horseback. The image recalls the Gore-Booths' Anglo-Irish gentry life at Lissadell, where Yeats knew Constance and her sister Eva in the 1890s. The question 'What voice more sweet than hers' sets the woman's earlier charm against her political shrillness, a contrast that later feminist critics have found condescending.

anchor: This man had kept a school
title: This man (Patrick Pearse)
short: Patrick Pearse (1879–1916), founder of St Enda's school, poet, and leader of the Rising, executed 3 May 1916.
body: Patrick (Pádraig) Pearse founded St Enda's (Scoil Éanna), a bilingual Irish school in Dublin, in 1908. He was a poet in Irish and English and an advocate of blood sacrifice for Irish freedom. He read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic outside the General Post Office on Easter Monday and was commander-in-chief of the rebel forces. He was executed by firing squad at Kilmainham Gaol on 3 May 1916. 'Rode our winged horse' means he wrote poetry (Pegasus being the poets' steed).

title: our winged horse
short: Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek myth, emblem of poetic inspiration.
body: Pegasus, the winged horse born from the blood of Medusa, struck the spring Hippocrene from Mount Helicon, the mountain of the Muses; later tradition made him the mount of poets and a symbol of poetic inspiration. 'Our' winged horse claims Pearse as a fellow poet. The understatement of the phrase ('rode') is typical of the stanza's mix of respect and reservation.

anchor: This other his helper and friend
title: his helper and friend (Thomas MacDonagh)
short: Thomas MacDonagh (1878–1916), poet, critic and teacher at St Enda's and University College Dublin, executed 3 May 1916.
body: Thomas MacDonagh taught with Pearse at St Enda's and lectured in English at University College Dublin; his critical study Literature in Ireland was published posthumously in 1916. He was a signatory of the Proclamation and commanded the garrison at Jacob's biscuit factory. Yeats knew him through literary circles and thought him 'coming into his force': his talent was just maturing. The phrase 'So sensitive his nature seemed, / So daring and sweet his thought' is the most affectionate tribute in the stanza.

title: This other man (John MacBride)
short: Major John MacBride (1868–1916), estranged husband of Maud Gonne, whom Yeats despised, yet includes in the poem.
body: John MacBride fought against the British in the Boer War with an Irish Brigade, married Maud Gonne in 1903, and separated from her in 1905 amid accusations of drunkenness and domestic abuse, which he denied. He joined the Rising almost by chance and was executed on 5 May 1916. 'He had done most bitter wrong / To some who are near my heart' refers to Gonne and her daughter Iseult. Yeats nonetheless numbers him 'in the song', a gesture of reluctant justice; Maud Gonne felt the poem unworthy of its subject, above all of MacBride.

title: the casual comedy
short: Life before the Rising is figured as an unplanned farce in which each man had a role he has now resigned.
body: The theatrical metaphor continues from 'motley': MacBride 'has resigned his part' (given up his role) in 'the casual comedy', the haphazard, unserious drama of everyday Dublin life. 'Casual' suggests both accident and lack of seriousness. Yeats, a man of the theatre as co-founder of the Abbey Theatre, uses the conceit to describe the transformation as a change of genre, from comedy to tragedy.

title: Transformed utterly
short: A variation of the refrain: MacBride is 'transformed', a change from the 'changed' of the other refrains.
body: In stanzas 1 and 4 the line reads 'changed, changed utterly'; in stanza 2 Yeats writes 'Transformed utterly', with the preceding line 'He, too, has been changed in his turn'. The variation emphasises that even the man Yeats despised has undergone a complete metamorphosis through his sacrifice. 'Transformed' carries a hint of religious transfiguration, appropriate to an Easter poem about death and new birth.

title: Enchanted to a stone
short: The single-minded revolutionaries' hearts are like a stone in a stream, unmoving amid the living flux of nature.
body: The third stanza turns from persons to a symbol. The hearts of those with 'one purpose alone' seem 'enchanted', as by a spell, into a stone that 'troubles' (disturbs) the 'living stream'. Around it, horse, rider, birds, clouds and moor-hens 'change' from minute to minute. The stone stands for fixed purpose, both heroic and inhuman: it gives the stream its form but cannot share its life. The image had a private dimension: In 1916 Yeats reportedly read the poem to Maud Gonne and urged her to put aside political fixity for the changing joy of life, and Gonne's later letter objected to its picture of the rebels' hearts as stone.

title: moor-hens … moor-cocks
short: Water birds of the stream, emblem of the procreative, changing life that continues around the stone.
body: The moorhen (Gallinula chloropus) is a small water bird of ponds and streams. The 'hens' calling 'to moor-cocks' bring sexual and seasonal life into the stanza, an image of the living, mating, changing world. The repeated 'Minute by minute' measures the time the natural world lives in, against the stone's unchanging state. The stanza's natural imagery may draw on Yeats's experience of Coole and Galway rivers.

title: Too long a sacrifice
short: A sacrifice prolonged too long can harden the heart: a reservation about the cost of revolutionary single-mindedness.
body: The fourth stanza opens with the poem's sharpest doubt: 'Too long a sacrifice / Can make a stone of the heart.' The sacrifice may be that of the revolutionaries, or the long political devotion of figures like Maud Gonne and Markievicz, or the centuries-long struggle of Ireland. Maud Gonne, in her letter of 3 November 1916, told Yeats bluntly that she did not like the poem and felt it unworthy of its subject. The question 'O when may it suffice?' asks when enough sacrifice will have been made; the answer is given to 'heaven', leaving 'our part' as mourning.

title: To murmur name upon name
short: The poet's role is like a mother's murmuring over a sleeping child: to name the dead tenderly.
body: Yeats assigns the judgement of the sacrifice to heaven and gives the living the task of commemoration: to 'murmur name upon name', as in a litany or roll-call. The simile of a mother naming her child 'when sleep at last has come / On limbs that had run wild' makes the dead into children asleep after wild play, a tender but also infantilising image. The speaker immediately corrects himself: 'No, no, not night but death', rejecting the consoling euphemism.

title: England may keep faith
short: The Home Rule Act of 1914 had been passed but suspended for the war; perhaps the deaths were 'needless'.
body: The Government of Ireland Act 1914, granting Ireland limited self-government (Home Rule), received royal assent in September 1914, but its operation was suspended for the duration of the war. Yeats asks whether the Rising was 'needless death' since England might have kept its promise. The question hangs unanswered: the poem neither affirms nor denies the necessity of the rebellion. After 1916 Home Rule was in practice overtaken by the War of Independence, and the act never came into force in the south.

title: excess of love / Bewildered them
short: Perhaps an excess of patriotic love confused the rebels to their deaths: the poem's final reservation before naming them.
body: Yeats suggests that the rebels' love of Ireland was so excessive that it 'bewildered' them (led them astray, confused them) 'till they died'. The phrase may be read as tribute (their love surpassed reason) or as criticism (their love was misplaced, a romantic folly). It may also glance at Pearse's doctrine of blood sacrifice. The lines that follow ('I write it out in a verse') assert the poet's own role: whatever the judgement, he will record their names.

title: MacDonagh and MacBride / And Connolly and Pearse
short: The four executed leaders named at last, including James Connolly, socialist leader of the Irish Citizen Army.
body: After withholding names throughout, Yeats now lists four of the executed men. Thomas MacDonagh, John MacBride and Patrick Pearse have been described in stanza 2; James Connolly (1868–1916), the labour leader and commander of the Irish Citizen Army, was so badly wounded that he was executed tied to a chair on 12 May 1916. The naming fulfils the promise to 'murmur name upon name'. The order (MacDonagh, MacBride, Connolly, Pearse) is shaped by rhyme ('Pearse / verse') rather than rank.

title: Wherever green is worn
short: Green, the colour of Irish nationalism, replaces the 'motley' of stanza 1; the dead will be remembered wherever it is worn.
body: Green is the traditional colour of Ireland and of Irish nationalism (the 'wearing of the green'). The line answers stanza 1's 'motley': the fool's costume has given way to the national colour. 'Now and in time to be' echoes liturgical formulas ('now and ever shall be'), giving the conclusion the weight of prayer. Yeats himself had reservations about green as a political symbol, which makes his use of it here more striking.
